In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prominence of a triconstituent compound depends on the prominence of its embedded compound.
the LCPR is not supported and that the placement and number of accents in triconstituent words depends on the prominence pattern and the number of accents in the embedded compound.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the prominence of trisegmental compounds depends on the prominence pattern within the embedded compound, and that prominence assignment in compounds is a function of prosodic prominence, not of syntactic branching.
the pitch contours of triconstituents are not determined by the branching direction of the whole compound, but by the prominence of the embedded compound.
the prominence pattern of compounds is not determined by the branching direction of the compounds, but by the prominence pattern of their embedded constituents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pitch contours of compounds are a rich and underutilized resource for the investigation of linguistic structure.
the pitch movements in triconstituent compound words can only be properly analyzed with a mixed-effects model.

prominence assignment to trisegmental compounds is not a lexical phenomenon, but is rather dependent on the phonetic and phonological properties of the embedded compounds, and thus on the phonology of the language in which these compounds occur.
